title: Coxinha
subtitle: Teardrop-shaped Brazilian chicken croquettes
excerpt: Crispy, teardrop-shaped croquettes filled with shredded chicken and cream cheese, coated in breadcrumbs and fried until golden. These are the most popular snack at Brazilian parties and bakeries. They take time and patience to shape, but the result is worth every step.
sourceNotes: Coxinha means little thigh in Portuguese and the croquette is shaped to resemble a chicken drumstick. The snack is believed to have originated in Sao Paulo in the nineteenth century and is now one of the most popular street foods and party snacks in Brazil, found in bakeries and snack bars throughout the country.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze shaped, unfried coxinha on a tray. Once solid, transfer to a bag. Fry from frozen, adding 3 to 4 minutes to the cooking time.
recipe.batchNotes: Make large batches and freeze before frying. suited to parties.

content.text: This recipe makes 20 coxinha and takes about 1 hour 40 minutes in total, including chilling time. The dough is made from chicken stock, which gives it savoury flavour and a smooth, pliable texture. Read the whole method before starting: coxinha have several stages and it helps to have everything laid out before you begin shaping.

The dough should feel like soft playdough: pliable but not sticky. If it sticks to your hands, add a little more flour. When shaping, flatten each piece into a circle, add a heaped teaspoon of filling, then gather the edges up and pinch them together at the top to form the teardrop. The pinched end is the point of the drumstick shape. Chill the shaped coxinha for at least 30 minutes before frying so they hold their shape in the oil.

Place the chicken thighs in a pot, cover with cold water and add salt. Bring to a simmer and cook for 25 minutes until cooked through. Remove the chicken and reserve 500ml of the cooking stock. Once cool enough to handle, shred the chicken finely, discarding skin and bones.

Fry the onion in a little oil in a pan over medium heat for 5 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add the shredded chicken, 150g cream cheese, the coriander and a good pinch of salt. Stir to combine, then set aside to cool.

To make the dough, bring the reserved 500ml chicken stock and 30g butter to the boil in a saucepan. Remove from the heat and tip in the 300g flour all at once. Stir vigorously with a wooden spoon until the mixture forms a smooth ball that pulls away from the sides. Leave to cool for 10 minutes.
Knead the dough briefly until smooth and pliable. Divide into 20 equal pieces. Set up your coating station: beaten eggs in one bowl and breadcrumbs in another.

Flatten each dough piece into a circle about 8cm across. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre. Bring the edges up around the filling and pinch firmly at the top to seal, forming a teardrop or pear shape. Smooth any cracks with damp fingers.
Dip each coxinha in beaten egg, let the excess drip off, then roll in breadcrumbs until fully coated. Place on a tray and refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Heat oil to 175C in a deep pan. Fry the coxinha in batches of 4 or 5 for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until deep golden brown. Drain on kitchen paper and serve hot.

attrs.symptom: Coxinha are bursting open in the oil
attrs.cause: Dough was not sealed properly, or they were not chilled before frying
attrs.fix: Make sure the seam is pinched firmly shut with no cracks. Chill for at least 30 minutes before frying. Overfilling also causes bursting; use no more than 1 heaped teaspoon of filling.

attrs.symptom: Dough is sticky and hard to shape
attrs.cause: The dough is too warm from the hot stock, or needs a little more flour
attrs.fix: Let the dough cool more before shaping, or refrigerate it for 15 minutes. Add flour a tablespoon at a time if it remains unworkable.

attrs.symptom: Coating is falling off during frying
attrs.cause: Too little egg coating or the breadcrumbs were not pressed firmly on
attrs.fix: Make sure each coxinha is fully dipped in egg with no dry patches, then press the breadcrumbs on firmly rather than just rolling. Double-coating (egg, breadcrumbs, egg again, breadcrumbs again) gives the strongest result.

content.text: Coxinha are sold at padarias and lanchonetes (snack bars) across Brazil from morning until night. In Sao Paulo, where they are said to have originated, you can find them on almost every corner. They are the go-to party food across the country and the thing Brazilian children ask for at birthday parties alongside brigadeiros. Making them at home takes time, but a tray of freshly fried coxinha goes a long way.
